summary: Reports on Comcast's experiences in a July 2008 technical trial of P4P, using iTracker technology to help peer-to-peer applications work better with ISP networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: An internet provider tried telling file-sharing programs which neighbors are close, so they would trade nearby and save road space.

subtitle: Results from Comcast's trial of P4P iTrackers to optimize peer-to-peer file sharing.

tldr.problem: Peer-to-peer (P2P) applications create large amounts of network traffic that often crosses ISP boundaries, increasing costs for internet providers and slowing downloads for users.
tldr.mechanism: Comcast deployed a P4P iTracker server that shares network topology information with P2P applications, allowing them to prefer local peers over distant ones, keeping traffic within the ISP's network.
tldr.outcome: The July 2008 trial with Pando Networks showed faster downloads for users, reduced external traffic by up to 80%, and demonstrated that ISPs can improve performance without revealing detailed network structure.

today: RFC 5632 is an Informational RFC documenting the results of a specific ISP trial. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The P4P concept was later considered by the IETF ALTO (Application Layer Traffic Optimization) working group as part of efforts to improve P2P and application performance in networks.

sections.title: Overview of P4P and the Trial
sections.content:
P4P stands for Proactive Network Provider Participation for P2P. The idea is that internet service providers can help peer-to-peer applications work more efficiently by sharing information about network topology. A P4P iTracker (information tracker) is a server maintained by an ISP that tells P2P applications where nearby peers are located in the network.

Comcast, a large U.S. cable broadband ISP, conducted a technical trial in July 2008 in cooperation with Pando Networks, Yale University, and other ISPs. The trial tested whether P4P iTrackers could help P2P swarms localize (keep data transfers local), reduce traffic flowing over expensive transit links, and improve download speeds for users. This RFC reports the results, which showed promise for both P2P users and ISPs.
sections.plainLanguage: A cable company tried letting file-sharing apps know where nearby users are, so apps would trade with neighbors instead of across the world. It worked: faster downloads and less clogged roads.

sections.title: How the Trial Worked
sections.content:
The trial distributed a 21-megabyte licensed video file using five different swarms (groups of P2P clients downloading together). One swarm used random peer selection (the control), and four swarms used different P4P iTracker configurations. Comcast deployed a P4P iTracker server in its production network.

When a P2P client joined the trial, it queried the pTracker (which manages the P2P network), which occasionally consulted the P4P iTracker to get network topology information. Based on that information, the pTracker would suggest an initial list of peers: 90% selected according to P4P topology guidance and 10% selected randomly. Peers could then discover additional peers through direct exchange.

Pando captured extended logging of all data transfers, including source and destination IP addresses and transfer volumes, allowing precise measurement of how traffic flowed through the network. Download speeds and completion rates were also measured for each swarm.
sections.plainLanguage: A file was shared across five groups. The control group traded randomly. The other four groups got advice from an iTracker about who was nearby. Researchers carefully measured how fast each group downloaded and where the traffic went.

sections.title: Three P4P iTracker Designs
sections.content:
Comcast tested three different designs for the P4P iTracker, each with a different level of detail and localization. The Fine Grain design mapped network topology down to optical transport nodes where cable modems connect, defining 1,182 different network segments. It was highly detailed but complex to maintain and took longer to create. Trial results showed it was actually less effective than simpler designs, likely because clients receiving very fine-grained locality had too much choice.

The Coarse Grain design used a summarized version: it mapped Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) to IP aggregates with weights reflecting peering costs and priority. It defined only 22 network segments and proved to be the most effective balance of complexity, manageability, and performance. Updates were simpler to automate, which helps keep the data current.

The Generic Weighted design was similar to Coarse Grain but used pre-determined weights designed by Yale researchers instead of Comcast-specific priorities. This design required about the same effort as Coarse Grain to set up.
sections.plainLanguage: Comcast built three maps: one super-detailed with 1,182 locations (too much detail), one medium with 22 areas (just right), and one with a standard template. The medium one worked best.

sections.title: Trial Results
sections.content:
During the trial, the Coarse Grain P4P configuration achieved download speeds 15% faster on average globally and 85% faster on the Comcast network compared to the random (control) swarm. Both Fine Grain and Generic Weighted showed similar improvements. Users also experienced fewer cancellations (1.77% to 2.22% for P4P swarms versus 3.17% for random).

Most striking was the impact on network traffic. P4P configurations reduced incoming internet traffic at peering points by an average of 80% compared to the random swarm. Outgoing traffic at peering points was reduced by 34%. This means much more of the traffic stayed within Comcast's network rather than crossing expensive transit links to other networks.

Interestingly, download activity within the Comcast network actually increased slightly with P4P (59 to 61 MB versus 56 MB for random), which is expected: peers were trading more locally. The trial involved approximately 1 million downloads across all five swarms, peaking at nearly 124,000 downloads per day and 57,000 concurrent peers.
sections.plainLanguage: Files downloaded 15% faster globally, 85% faster in Comcast's network. Internet bills (external traffic) dropped 80%. Local trades went up. Users were happier and canceled fewer downloads.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Implications
sections.content:
A key finding was that an ISP can improve P2P performance without exposing detailed internal network structure. The Coarse Grain design revealed much less network detail than the Fine Grain, yet performed better. This addresses security concerns: fine-grained network topology information could theoretically be exploited by attackers, but the optimal P4P configuration provides only aggregate network information.

The P4P iTracker shares only network topology information—the map of where segments are and how they relate. It does not reveal which P2P clients are downloading which content, which would be a privacy concern. The RFC notes that if P4P mechanisms are standardized, they should probably be opt-in for P2P users, so users can choose whether to use the system.

The trial also showed that ISPs can operate P4P iTrackers relatively inexpensively on small servers, making broad ISP adoption feasible. However, the RFC emphasizes that P4P provides the most value when many ISPs deploy it; a single ISP's benefit is limited if P2P swarms span multiple networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISP didn't reveal secret network details, just a neighborhood map. It didn't snoop on what people downloaded. Users could opt in or out. The system was cheap to run.
